title: Refuses to Commit to Peaceful Transfer of Power
description_short: When asked if he would accept a peaceful transfer of power after the 2020 election, Trump refused to commit and blamed mail ballots.
description_medium: At a Sept. 23, 2020, White House news conference, Donald Trump declined to commit to a peaceful transfer of power if he lost the election. He complained that mail ballots were a “disaster” and said there would be a “continuation” rather than a transfer if they were removed. His campaign argued the question assumed he would lose.
description_long: At a White House news conference on Sept. 23, 2020, President Donald Trump was asked whether he would accept a peaceful transfer of power if he lost the election, “win, lose or draw.” He answered, “Well, we’ll have to see what happens,” then criticized ballots as a “disaster.” When the reporter asked about rioting, Trump said, “Get rid of the ballots,” and added that there would be no transfer, but a “continuation.” He appeared to be referring to mail-in ballots, which he had repeatedly attacked without evidence as vulnerable to widespread fraud. The Biden campaign responded that voters would decide the election and that the government could remove trespassers from the White House. Trump’s campaign said the question assumed he would lose, which he disputed. The exchange left open whether he would accept defeat and a change in administration after the vote. It drew attention to the role of mail voting and the peaceful transfer of power weeks before the November election.

preserved_fields.title: Refuses to Commit to Peaceful Transfer of Power
preserved_fields.description_short: When asked if he would accept a peaceful transfer of power after the 2020 election, Trump refused to commit and blamed mail ballots.

notes: The linked CNBC report supplies the question, Trump’s replies, his reference to ballots and the campaign responses. The account does not infer what Trump would have done after a loss.

title: Tender Age Facilities — Babies and Toddlers Separated
description_short: Tender Age Facilities — Babies and Toddlers Separated
description_medium: During the Trump administration’s family-separation policy, infants and toddlers were among the children separated from parents and placed in “tender age” shelters. Shelter workers described very young children crying inconsolably and lacking adequate comfort. The American Academy of Pediatrics warned that separation from caregivers could harm children’s development.

title: Trump Pardons 143 Allies Including Flynn, Stone, Manafort, Bannon
description_short: Trump Pardons 143 Allies Including Flynn, Stone, Manafort, Bannon
description_medium: In his final hours as president on Jan. 20, 2021, Donald Trump granted clemency to 143 people: 73 pardons and 70 commutations. Steve Bannon was among those pardoned while awaiting trial on federal fraud charges. The total includes sentence commutations, and other named allies received clemency on different dates.
description_long: In the final hours of his presidency on Jan. 20, 2021, Donald Trump granted clemency to 143 people, according to the White House list reported by NBC News. That total consisted of 73 pardons and 70 commutations, which have different legal effects: pardons forgive federal offenses, while commutations reduce or end sentences without erasing convictions. Steve Bannon received a pardon while awaiting trial on charges connected to the We Build the Wall fundraising project. Prosecutors alleged that the campaign diverted donated money for personal expenses; Bannon denied wrongdoing. Trump had publicly distanced himself from Bannon after his arrest. Other recipients included Lil Wayne, Kodak Black, fundraiser Elliott Broidy and former Detroit Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick, each with a different case history. The 143 figure counts all clemency actions, not 143 pardons, and the total does not mean every recipient was a political ally. Michael Flynn, Roger Stone and Paul Manafort received clemency in earlier actions, not as part of this final-day list.

notes: Needs context: NBC confirms 143 final-day clemency grants comprised 73 pardons and 70 commutations, and that Bannon was pardoned. Proposed correction: narrow the title to the final-day grants and separate Bannon’s pardon from prior grants to other named figures.
